title: Netflix's Big Bet: One model to rule recommendations: Yesu Feng, Netflix

summary: Yesu Feng outlines Netflix's foundation model strategy for personalization, motivated by three levels of diversity in recommendation: rows, entities (movies, TV, games, live streaming), and pages (homepage, search, kids, mobile). Historically, each use case spawned independent specialized models with extensive duplication in feature engineering. Around four years ago, Netflix hypothesized centralizing user representation learning into one transformer-based foundation model, driven by scaling laws and high leverage across downstream systems. The four-layer architecture includes event representation, embedding transformation (ID + semantic content for cold-start), transformer layers, and multi-faceted objective/loss layers. Netflix validated scaling laws over ~2-2.5 years, scaling from ~10M profiles to ~1B parameters, stopping due to latency constraints requiring distillation. On the serving side, the foundation model consolidates data, representation, and model layers, turning downstream application models into thinner layers built on top of the FM. Three consumption patterns integrate the FM: (1) as a subgraph within downstream models replacing sequence transformer towers, (2) pushing out content and member embeddings to a centralized embedding store for wide use beyond personalization, and (3) extracting and fine-tuning or distilling the model for strict latency requirements. Over ~1.5 years, Netflix observed both AB test wins and infrastructure consolidation, validating the big bets: scalable model quality, high leverage via centralized learning, and faster innovation velocity for new applications. Current directions include universal representation for heterogeneous entities via semantic IDs, generative retrieval for collection recommendation with multi-step decoding handling business rules naturally, and faster adaptation through prompt tuning with soft tokens. Netflix also uses graph models (knowledge graph embeddings for cold-start) and reinforcement learning (sparse rewards guiding collection generation). Frame-level video embeddings are not yet incorporated but represent a future trend.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Diversity of Netflix Recommendation Needs
sections.summary: Feng introduces Netflix's recommendation landscape with three levels of diversity: rows (genres, trending, originals), entities (movies, TV, games, live streaming, expanding content space), and pages (homepage, search, kids homepage, mobile feed with different layouts).

sections.title: Traditional Model Proliferation and Its Problems
sections.summary: Historically, diverse needs led to many independently-built specialized models with overlapping objectives. This caused duplication in feature and label engineering, making maintenance difficult and reducing innovation velocity and leverage.

sections.title: Foundation Model Hypothesis
sections.summary: About four years ago during the pandemic, Netflix hypothesized centralizing user representation learning into one transformer-based foundation model. Two sub-hypotheses: scaling laws apply to recommendation, and integrating the foundation model creates high leverage across all downstream models.

sections.title: Data, Tokenization, and Model Architecture
sections.summary: Tokenization for recommendation differs from LLMs: each token is a rich interaction event with fields (when/where/what), not a single ID. The four-layer architecture includes event representation, embedding transformation (ID + semantic content for cold-start), transformer layers (hidden state as user representation), and multi-faceted objective/loss layers supporting multi-task learning, weights, rewards, and masking for fine-tuning.

sections.title: Scaling Law Validation
sections.summary: Netflix validated that scaling laws apply to recommendation over ~2-2.5 years, scaling from ~10M profiles to ~1B model parameters with continued gains. Stopped due to stringent latency cost requirements; further scaling requires distillation.

sections.title: LLM-Borrowed Techniques
sections.summary: Three key techniques borrowed from LLMs: multi-token prediction (from DeepSeek, improving robustness and long-term focus), multi-layer representation (layer-wise supervision, self-distillation, multi-layer aggregation for stable user representation), and long context window handling (truncated sliding window, sparse attention, progressive training, parallelism).

sections.title: Serving and Applications Introduction
sections.summary: Feng shifts to the serving and application side, describing the algorithm stack for personalization before the foundation model was introduced, where many models were independently developed.

sections.title: FM Consumption Patterns and Integration
sections.summary: The foundation model consolidates data, representation, and model layers. Downstream application models become thinner layers built on top of the FM rather than standalone full-fledged models trained from scratch. Three main consumption patterns are described.

sections.title: Three Consumption Patterns
sections.summary: Pattern 1: FM integrated as a subgraph within downstream models, replacing existing sequence transformer towers. Pattern 2: Push out content and member embeddings to a centralized embedding store, enabling use beyond personalization by analytics teams. Pattern 3: Extract and fine-tune or distill the FM for applications with strict latency requirements.

sections.title: Results and Big Bets Validation
sections.summary: Over ~1.5 years, Netflix accumulated wins: blue bars show applications with FM incorporated, green bars show AB test wins. This validated the big bets—scalable model quality, infrastructure consolidation, high leverage via centralized learning, and faster innovation velocity as new applications can fine-tune the FM to launch first experiences.

sections.title: Current and Future Directions
sections.summary: Three current directions: (1) universal representation for heterogeneous entities via semantic IDs as Netflix expands content types, (2) generative retrieval for collection recommendation with multi-step decoding naturally handling business rules and diversity, (3) faster adaptation through prompt tuning with soft tokens borrowed from LLMs, allowing inference-time behavior changes.

sections.title: Q&A Session
sections.summary: Audience Q&A covers: expanding FM beyond recommendation to capture user taste on and off platform; graph models used via knowledge graph embeddings for cold-start and a dedicated team; reinforcement learning for sparse rewards guiding collection generation; embeddings exposed downstream and consuming upstream GNN embeddings; and frame-level video embeddings not yet incorporated but identified as a future trend.
